title: Your reading plan
hookLine: choose one text to keep reading after the summit
tomorrow: seventy days a guest. what does a good guest say at the door?

lines: A CHILD'S VOICE OVER A WALL.
A MAN UNDER A FIG TREE.
cards: A child's voice drifts over a garden wall, chanting the same words again and again. On the other side, under a fig tree, a teacher of speech, learned and restless, sits weeping, unable to change his life.
The voice says: "Take up and read; Take up and read." In his Latin, tolle lege. You can't keep every book; this man was about to find the one he'd keep.

teach.b: The man is Augustine; this reading opened in his garden, and now it closes there. He tells the story in his Confessions. He can't remember any children's game with those words, so he takes them as a command.

He goes back to the bench where he left a book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads the first passage his eyes fall on: not in rioting and drunkenness, not in strife and envying, but "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ."

teach.h: ONE PASSAGE, AND NO NEED TO READ ON.
teach.b: He writes that he didn't want to read further, and had no need to. A light seemed to pour into his heart, and the doubt was gone. Notice the senses in it.

teach.h: A VOICE, A WEIGHT, A PAGE.
teach.b: A child's voice over a wall. The weight of a book in the hand. One passage, not a library.

Some Christian teachers point to Augustine's garden as a picture of a way of reading: scripture taken up not as information, but as a word addressed to the reader, a passage at a time, read slowly enough to change a life.
A detail worth keeping: the voice that turned Augustine around came from a child next door, and he never says whose it was. That's the companion-text idea.
One book, kept close, opened often.
Choosing it isn't turning away from the rest of the shelf.

how: Augustine's 'take up and read' (Confessions 8.12) is retold in Christian teaching about reading scripture slowly and personally; some readers, on any path, keep one text close and read a little of it each day.

o: a list of every book you plan to finish
one text you keep reading, slowly, for years
a book someone else assigns you to study

p: put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ

s: Augustine read Paul's letters cover to cover that day
he read one passage and writes that he had no need to read further.
Augustine never says whose voice he heard
he couldn't recall any game with those words, and took them as a command.
choosing one companion text means rejecting the rest
it's how one book becomes a friend; the others stay on their shelves.

games.q: a friend plans to 'read all the scriptures this year' and is already lost by week two. what does Augustine's garden suggest?
o: take up one and read it slowly, a passage at a time.
speed-read them all; the point is to cover the ground.
wait for a sign before opening any of them.
games.why: Augustine read one passage and stopped: in his story, depth comes from a single page taken to heart.

practice: Pick up a book you might keep reading, any book that matters to you, or open one text on your phone. Feel its weight, open it anywhere, and read one line out loud, slowly, twice.
Then close it and rest your hand on the cover for the rest of the time.
